title: Practice Beyond Preferences
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The Soto Zen dharma talk emphasizes the importance of living in the present moment, free from attachment to thoughts, emotions, or expectations. By cultivating awareness through meditation and embracing life's imperfections, one can find happiness and stability, rather than trying to control or achieve a specific state. This approach requires faith and trust in the practice itself, letting go of need for control and planning, and instead discovering freedom and presence in everyday life.

We're trying to have a sort of spiritual community center in downtown Bellingham.
The idea of today, as you probably figured out, is to offer an experience that has all the pieces of a formal Zen meditation retreat but with a lot of guidance and instruction.
I hope all these words don't get to be too overwhelming.
That was a very sophisticated and elegant explanation of the posture, more than we usually do.

But yeah, when you start to break it down, it just seems heinously complicated, like, wow.
The point of it all is to provide us some structure and some container for a deep investigation of what this life is.

*Enough.

*If not this breath, this sitting here.

We have refused, again and again, until now.
Until now.
Enough.

This opening to the life.*
*We have refused, again and again, until now.
Until now.*
This is a good, actually he's not a Zen student, but it's a great Zen poem because it's dramatic, you know, like, what?

But as we investigate through spiritual practice, and I'm sure you're all finding this, there are these little ways that we resist.
We don't quite want this life, maybe a slightly improved version.
Only this were different about our personality, our partner, our job, our...
You fill in the blank.
Zen came to America with a great fit of enthusiasm in the 1950s and 1960s.
At the time, some of the proponents of Zen described it as a very radical, philosophical leaping beyond all philosophy and concepts.
And so now we have Zen as a marketing slogan for some kind of sensibility.

But actually, as we've practiced Zen in America these last 50 or 60 years, and none of us here have been practicing 50 or 60 years, but some of us 20 or 30 or 35, we've gradually realized it's a much richer matrix than some cold puzzling jumping out of life.
It really is just life.
And it comes to us in the container of Buddhism, and it actually is a religion.
I'm sorry, I didn't want to get the bad news out of the way if you're a non-religion person: Zen actually is a religion because it's Zen Buddhism.
So it's a particular emphasis.
And just like Christianity, there are many different Buddhisms.
It's debatable how we define things and divide things up.
Is a Pentecostal meeting in the living room of a farmhouse in Iowa the same as a Catholic cathedral in France?
Both Christianity, right?
It can be a little bit the same with Buddhism.
You could go to different Buddhist places in America and in Asia, and it could feel like, wow, this is completely different.
Each one has its own style and presentation and cultural accoutrement.
Zen Buddhism comes from Japan, so it brings with it a bit of a Japanese aesthetic.
You might have noticed unusual clothing and things lined up very carefully.
Which of this is the essence of Buddhist teaching and which is Japanese culture, we have no idea.
So we take what we have been given and we work with it as best we can and make some modifications as we go along.
But all of it references back to Shakyamuni Buddha, the historical Buddha, more or less 500 years before the birth of Christ.
Nobody knows exactly when he was born.
And his big question is really all of our big question.
That is: how can we make sense of living this life?

How can we use this powerful mind and this incredible range of emotion that we have as human beings in such a way that we're happy and enjoy our life and can be helpful to others, so that we're not destabilized and confused and really suffering just from the very nature of our personhood?
One way to look at that is, I think, obvious in our context.
Probably all of us have a pretty good confidence that we're going to have all the food we need today.
We have some level of material stability.
We probably, maybe all of us, have a roof over our head tonight.
There might be a few people a little shaky on that.
So our essential human needs are met in this context of living in Bellingham, Washington.
And so the question that we don't think about, we're busy, and maybe you are thinking about this, or you're here, is: why are we not deliriously happy and content every moment of our life?
What is this discontent, this feeling, even when things are going great?
Why are we so vulnerable to being so easily upset when somebody looks at us funny or writes something a little confusing in an email?
Or we don't get that job, or the job we love disappears, whatever.
Why is that?
That really was the Buddhist question.
The myth of his life is a setup to explore this question.

He was a very pampered prince and everything was provided, so he had the best possible material conditions for his time and place, which in a way, being in America in the 21st century, is exactly the same.
We live in a palace.
We don't notice, but we do.
And yet there was something in him that wasn't happy.
There are different ways that the story is told.
One is that the harsh realities of having a human temporary body were a big thing, to realize that we're all going to get sick, that we're all aging, and that we're all going to die.
There's a way we hold that in abeyance at a distance, and somehow, the way the story of the Buddha is told, he was not able to do that.
It was so immediate and so graphically true and frightening for him when he realized, oh, my God, how can we live knowing that we're dying?
How can this be?
So this is our question: how do we appreciate this life the way it actually is?
We've figured out by now that we can't create another life, that we just get this life in this body that's always in limitations.
So how can we appreciate that and enjoy that even when it's not going our way?

One of the ways that he explained that, a central point and the central point that Zen emphasizes, is that there's a quality of mind that arises very quickly in every moment, probably, in ourselves, in meditation today: a quality of mind that is grabbing for something or pushing something away, a quality of mind that's jumping here and there, left and right, in and out, up and down, that isn't stable and isn't accepting the actual reality of this moment as it arises.
Many things cascade from this grabbiness of mind, and one of them is the idea that we're who we think we are, this whole creation of an identity.
Thus we have massive amounts of Eastern and Western philosophy exploring identity: what is this identity?
Is the me I think I am really the whole me that there is, or is there really a me here, or am I walking around just with a big bag of assumptions?
And when we have the frequent miscommunications that we have with each other, is that why?
Because actually you're in a different reality than I am.
What the Buddha suggested is that we should really study this working of the mind experientially.
Not just talk about it or think about it or read books about it, but actually explore, moment by moment, breath by breath, what this experience of being a person in a body with a mind is.
And notice that as we start that exploration, this mind with its grabby quality doesn't want to rest here in this actual moment.

Basically, when we're running around living our life, we essentially have three different types of mind, so when we're running around living our life we essentially have three questions that we're constantly asking ourselves, maybe four.
Let's see if this is true for you.
I think it is.
We're asking ourselves, what's going to happen next?
Does that have some resonance?
What's going to happen next?
When you come to a strange meditation center you might have that question: will you be okay?
So, what's next?
And we're constantly asking ourselves, what just happened?
What was that?
Or what happened long ago?
Looking into the past, right?
What happened in my childhood?
Is that why I am the way I am now?
What happened?
So: what's coming next?
What happened?
And then we're constantly asking ourselves, how am I doing?
Not too good.
Do these have resonance for you?
There are other questions we're constantly asking ourselves too, but they all seem to extend from those, like, how is she doing?
What is she doing next?
So the suggestion from Buddhism that Zen really emphasizes is, instead of trying to answer those questions, let's change the question.
Let's actually just change the question, and return to the question: what's happening now?
That's a lot of words.
Maybe just: what is this?
Or: what is it?
Or just that feeling of asking a question.

Through these teachings and meditation instructions, which we just got a big batch of and I'll give you a few more, through these techniques of Buddhism, Buddhist awareness technologies that have been cooked up over thousands of years, we add some practices, some things that we actually do with our body and mind regularly in our daily life, maybe at a place like this with other people, maybe on our own, or some of both, that support us in returning to this question of what's happening now.
This is not to deny the power of our thinking, and not to deny that we exist, or to go off on some weird philosophical trip about all this.
It's just to recognize that too much energy into these questions, what's happening next, what just happened, how am I doing, et cetera, just feeds the beast, you know what I mean?
It just makes us more crazy and less content.
These are sometimes important questions, so sometimes we need to ask the question, what am I doing next?
What is the next thing to do in my life?
Should I go back to school?
Should I get a job?
Should I take up Zen Buddhism?
These are not invalid questions, but the level of energy that goes into them seems to create a lot of trouble.
And so the ritual and practice container, the strongest medicine that we have to offer you here from Soto Zen Buddhism, is this practice of sitting all day.
That's our theme today: how to do this practice of sitting all day so that it will be helpful and not just driving you nuts.
Not just another new thing where you're like, what's happening next?
What just happened?
How am I doing?
Of course we would bring the same questions to everything we do, right?
Because the mind is conditioned from 20, 30, 50, 60, 70 years of asking these questions.
And in the Buddha's frame, actually many lifetimes before that maybe too, we've been asking these questions.
Do you have any answers yet?
Why do you keep asking?
The sitting all day is helpful in a lot of ways, as a carefully designed setup.
The central piece of it is the sitting meditation.
As Talus and Nancy mentioned, the center of sitting meditation in this particular school of Buddhism is awareness of breath in the body.
In one sense, the breath is just another physiological process.
So why is it any more important than the heartbeat, or that your fingernails are growing?
But the breath seems to be helpful in a lot of ways, and the recognition of that is actually embedded in language.
In English, which comes ultimately from the Aryan languages of India, we have words like inspiration, respiration, aspiration.
There's a sense of the breath being in the middle.
The breath is in the middle of our deepest wishes as a human being.
The breath is in the middle of the body.
And the breath is in the middle of this moment.
Since it's a more or less automatic process, you don't have to think about it to breathe, thank goodness.
If we actually are aware of how the breath feels right now in this moment, we're connecting to something that's happening now.
So it's a physical marker of the present moment that is always with us.
We don't have to remember to bring it in our backpack.
It's always in the middle of the body until we die, and then we don't need it anymore.
So we put a lot of emphasis on awareness of breathing, but not to become an expert at breath awareness, or an athlete.
There's a way that we approach every endeavor, with those three questions, right?
That leads us to want to get good, either get really good at something or be really upset with ourselves because we're not good at something.
So we're going to practice today with awareness of breathing, but when we forget to practice awareness of breathing, this is not actually a failure.
Failure and success are that same kind of grabbing mind again.
So our idea in using breath awareness as a marker and a tool includes forgetting.
It actually includes losing awareness.
Because when we lose awareness, and there's some support around this, we notice, we remember where we are, and we look around and say, "Oh my gosh, I'm in a meditation hall.
These are the people here, and oh, awareness of breathing, that's what we're doing."
So there's a returning to awareness.
That's really the secret sauce of practice: this returning to awareness.
One way to look at it is, the more often you forget, the better, because you have more opportunities to return to awareness.
You could think of this as building a spiritual muscle, I guess, but that again sounds acquisitive.
Then you want to know, "How am I doing?
Is my muscle strong yet?"
So that's not it either.
But it's this opportunity of return that seems to be so helpful in stabilizing our heart and opening up our life.
The sitting meditation practice is central to the sitting all day that we do.
It's central to practice every day if you get into that.
If you come back here during our regular schedule, we have five times a week that we do this meditation, and our friends in the Insight Meditation Group have two or three.
So there are quite a few opportunities to come back.
In those meetings of one or two hours, sitting meditation is also central.
If you divide up the amount of time, most of the time is spent in sitting meditation.
But that sitting meditation is understood to be not really different from the rest of our activity.
This is an important point, and it's another thing that Zen really emphasizes: it's not just about getting good at sitting, and then somehow the rest of your life will take care of itself.

It's about taking on a whole package or system, I guess, which is starting to lead us through, and will continue as we go on today: how you stand, how you hold your hands, how you walk, sitting down, getting up.
So this awareness we cultivate in sitting meditation, awareness of breathing, awareness of body, through the course of sitting all day, we can practice a continuity of practice.
And you can watch yourself and see.
That's another thing, we have this great opportunity when we forget.
You can watch what the quality of your effort is, and whether your effort is very jaggy.
It might be that the sitting meditation posture takes a little getting used to.
I'm sure it does, actually.
There's a creative engagement for some years of figuring out which props and which way to sit, and how to work with your body.
And like Nancy was telling us, how much to breathe with discomfort and how much wind to move, and all this.
So there's a little project there.

But one thing I want to suggest that you look for today, after our lunch and our lunch break, when we'll have a few periods of meditation one after the other without all this talking: look at what happens as the meditation period goes along, and as the bell finally rings at the end.
Even that word "finally" is a little loaded.
As the bell rings at the end, is there a sense of, "Whew, what's next?"
Right?
And then you're not...
So that's a losing of awareness, and a losing of this possibility of a continuity of practice.

The bell ringing is just marking a change in posture, not an ending of anything.
In other words, the way we understand meditation is that it actually doesn't start and stop ever.
It's just different postures that we take on in different contexts.
So the meditation just continues.
The posture changes.

The most direct and straightforward way to practice awareness of breathing, which we'd like you to try today, actually sounds mechanical.
It sounds like something an engineer would have made up, but it's a very ancient practice.
And that is to actually count your breaths.
To actually count your breaths.
The way it works is, once you've established the posture as was described to us, you can take a few breaths and feel your breathing.
If it's possible to feel the breathing in the center of the body, that's recommended, but wherever you can feel it is the important thing.
Maybe you feel it a little more in the chest.
Some kinds of Buddhism, they feel the breath in the nose.
That's okay too.
But find the breath as a physical sensation, not as an idea.
Then notice that there's inhalation and exhalation.
It's funny giving meditation instruction, because they're not idiots.
They know there's inhalation and exhalation.
But are we really aware of this?
Are we really aware of this?
So in this context, really being aware: "Okay, I can really feel the inhalation.
I can really feel the exhalation.
They're different.
The whole body changes in various ways."
So I'm feeling that.
And then on the next exhalation, you can just count to yourself, "one."
You notice the inhalation go by, and you count to yourself "two" with the next exhalation.

Should you get to ten, you can just return to one.

You can try that too if you like.
How that's really useful is that it makes it pretty obvious if the mind is drifting off into memory, to thoughts, to planning, to some dreamy state where you can't really tell what's going on.
Or maybe a strong sensation has gotten a hold of the attention, or an emotion has gotten a hold of the attention.
That's fine, but it's pretty easy to recognize: "Oh, I don't know what number I'm on.

So this is a useful practice, this breath counting.
Like I said, it sounds almost silly.

The important part, as I was saying before, is the spirit of coming back.
Falling off the numbers is not like one demerit.
After a hundred, they're probably not going to let you here anymore, but no, it's like, "Oh, just returning."
And then in that moment of return, you just notice what that is for you.
Because we forget things and remember things all day, right?
Every day.
We're always forgetting things.
Is that a failure?
How many times did you fail already today?
Or is it just the way the mind works?
Is it just the natural functioning of mind?
So just return with as little extra story as we can.
If a strong story emerges around this practice, then you can acknowledge that and then just return.
Maybe in some other talk I'll talk more about different levels of ways of practicing awareness of breathing, but there's a whole bunch of different ones.
The counting is a good starting place and a good ending place and a good returning place.
I did nothing but counting.
Maybe I just never asked if there was anything else available, but I did nothing but breath counting for, I don't know, maybe ten or twelve years.
Then finally, I remember I did go to a teacher and I said, "The breath counting just feels very rigid and tight, and I don't know if that's really helping me."
And she said, "Oh, really?
Maybe it's gotten a little automatic, the breath counting.
Why don't you count backwards now?"
So I counted backwards for, I don't know, two or three years.
So we're not in a hurry.
We're not in a hurry.
We're not really trying to achieve anything.
Because if we were, what is that feeding?
The same questions, right?
"How am I doing?
What's the next practice?
I'm done with that practice.
Aren't I good, [unclear: "Laura"]?
Oh, my God, I can't believe I'm still doing this.
Maybe I should try [unclear: "Tibetan moves"]."
Nothing wrong with that, but it's not exactly what seems to be helpful.

So what's underlying all this, and what I'm trying to say and make jokes about, is cultivating a kind of stability and a really radical acceptance that whatever is happening now is absolutely what needs to be happening right now.
I'm making a gentle effort.
I'm working with my life.
But I'm really trying to return to a sense of what's happening now.
What is this now?
From there, there's a stable ground.
Sometimes they call that the mind ground, this stable ground.
From there, we can live our life, and that includes making changes.
I'm not saying it doesn't.
But it may be easier to live our life and make the changes we need to make if we're not reevaluating our entire life every two seconds.
Now, this all-day sitting.
We use a smattering of Japanese words, so that in addition to all these movements, it takes getting used to.
The all-day sitting is called sesshin, sesshin.
It's made out of two characters.
The first means to touch.
The second means the heart and the mind; they have one word for the heart and the mind.
So the point of it is to touch the heart or the mind on this moment.
They did not use a word for improve or correct or better the mind.
It doesn't even mean calm the mind.
We used to think it meant, we misunderstood this for quite a few years, we used to think it meant to gather the mind.
We used to go to the intro talk and they'd always say sesshin means to gather the mind.
But it actually doesn't mean that.
It's a misunderstanding.
It means to touch in some way this mind, this heart.
And so there's a sense of faith here.
Like all religion, Buddhism is not without faith.
It's a faith that we explore experientially.
So it's not a sort of dogma.
We don't tell you what to believe.
There's no brochure that says the ten things a Buddhist should believe.
And we do have that in Christianity.
What's wrong with that?
We don't have that.
But we have some faith in the actual practice itself and in just being stable, just touching this heart, touching this mind.
That that is inherently healing and liberating.
And that there's a quality of the human animal, the human spiritual, psychological, emotional, everything animal, that's self-healing.
That we can relax a little more.
We don't have to work so hard to try to fix everything.
And faced with a short day like today, maybe it's a little intimidating.
I don't know.
Like, you're really going to be here till 5:30?
Ooh.
But maybe it's like, well, they're going to talk us through it, and we'll have breaks and all this.
So maybe it's not too intimidating.
But we also have retreats of three days and retreats of seven days.
So I'd like just to plant a few seeds for later, mostly.
Maybe you'll use them today, because it's important to your happiness.

When we're faced with something that seems like it's going to be really difficult, like running a marathon or having a baby or I don't know what, think of something difficult, driving when we're tired, the mind likes to make a strategy, right?
And in some way life is this vast collection of strategies.
You meet people who are really bound by their strategies, people like that.
There's a sort of tightness sometimes that emerges from so much strategy.
So faced with a lengthy period of day after day or hour after hour of a quiet meditation retreat, naturally you want to come up with a strategy.
And I'm going to tell you what the best strategy is.
You probably guessed it already.
The best strategy is not to have a strategy.
Didn't you guess that?
The best strategy is, when a desire for strategy arises, and what's next?
How am I going to survive?
When these thoughts arise, to see, oh, that's a really persuasive thought.
Maybe there's some fear under that thought.
Maybe some anger.
And to see if you can just return to breathing.
Again, it's not so much solving and answering these questions, these powerful thoughts, but working with attention, shifting the context, shifting the ground.
And it can be surprisingly liberating to have a time in your life when you can try to let go of strategy, try to let go of planning, let go of figuring everything out.
It takes some trust in the tradition and some trust in the organizers, so you might want to hang around a little bit, make sure they're trustworthy before you sign up for the seven-day gig.
But if you can really trust the situation, then there's a tremendous freedom, which is the reverse of how we usually describe freedom in American parlance.
We describe freedom as having the maximum number of choices, getting to do whatever we want.
That's freedom.

But what we've discovered little by little over the years, the people are still around anyway, I guess the people who maybe don't agree aren't here anymore, is that there's a tremendous freedom also in letting go of choices, letting go of being the boss, which is not a passive thing either.
It's a very active engagement, but it's engagement with the present moment as it's emerging.
You don't need to be the one who figures out how to improve Zen Buddhism today.
You don't need to be the one to figure out, and you've got to work with your body and all this.
I'm not saying there's no adjusting.
There's plenty of adjusting.
But there's a way that the mind can really grab onto a strategy to where it really just makes you tight, and then there's a lot more suffering.
My famous example of this is the first seven-day retreat I did.
Many have heard this story, but it's funny.
My strategy was to look at the schedule, and it was a fairly intense schedule.
We got up at four in the morning or something like that, and sat ten or eleven or twelve periods of meditation, longer than the ones we're doing here today.
That's why I'm pretty comfortable with math.
So I looked at that schedule, and pretty much at a glance I could calculate there were about 84 meditation periods or something like that.
So I started counting them down one by one.
The bell would ring, and instead of trying to practice this continuity of awareness like I was telling you, nobody told me about that, or maybe I didn't hear it, I would just say, okay, 79 to go.
Now, if it happens that in that moment you're feeling okay, then, oh, okay, 79 to go.

But if it happens that in that moment you're feeling really wretched, and your back hurts, and your mind is just racing, and you're doubting that you can do this, and then you come here, then that number is like a [unclear: "great legend"] to the head. 79!
No!
So that's a silly example of a strategy, but I actually did this.
And it seems like a sensible strategy, like if you're running a marathon you might be counting down the miles, but maybe that's not a good strategy then either, I don't know.
We have all these ways that we measure, and evaluate, and reevaluate, and reevaluate our evaluation.
So there's a real freedom that can be experientially validated in this cooked-up, thousand-year-old Japanese-style way of sitting around with a bunch of people.
That's strange but true.
And underlying all of this grabbiness is this sense of really wanting, in a hard-wired way almost, to pick and choose what I want and what I don't want.
So that's the other thing that's available through this experience of practice: to see what would actually happen if I set that down.
And it's not so easy to do.
Maybe it's impossible to do.
And so there's not exactly attainment or a measurable result either, because the minute we're involved in measuring a result, that's just another strategy.
But there's a famous poem in Zen that starts, *The great way is not difficult.
Just set aside picking and choosing.* That's all you've got to do.
But if you watch your mind, you see that's not so easy.
Still, I think little by little over time there's a sense of stability, a sense of being a little less reactive, a little more open, a little warmer maybe.
But being a person is all process and no result, right?
So you could practice meditation for 50 years and still get really pissed off at somebody, right?
But maybe less than you would have.
Who knows?
It's really hard to know.
We can't do an experiment with a control with our life, right?
We can't have the one person who didn't take on Zen meditation see how they do.
We have one version of me and the other version of me that did, and see which one's better.
We just have to take our guess at how to spend our time, how to spend our energy, how to spend our life.
And so what we often recommend about Zen practice is, try it for a while, a couple of months maybe.
See if it feels right.
There's a little bit of getting over the initial strangeness of it all, but once you're through that, does this feel right?
Does this feel like something that will really help my life?
And if it does, why wouldn't you do that?
And this is not what you need to help your life.
What are you doing to help your life?
So let me end with a quirky Zen story, because that's the other great thing about Zen.
We have access to a tremendous number of strange and quirky stories.

Not to go too long into that, but that's the other aspect of Zen that differentiates it a little bit from Buddhism as a whole: a little less emphasis on the Buddha's systematic teachings about meditation and how to go about this.

All of this happens in the context of community.
That's part of why we're making a big deal either.

It all happens in the context of community and encounter.
And the Zen stories, which can be a little odd, are because of their style always stories of encounter.
And out of that encounter, something emerges.
We're encountering each other right now.

*Zhao Zhou, instructing the assembly, said, "The supreme way is not difficult.
